dataset.name: Soil Chamber Fluxes (CO2 and CH4) across a catena in the Luquillo Experimental Forest, Puerto Rico
description: Wet tropical forest soils contribute significantly to global emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). Landscape topography largely influences the rate of CO2 versus CH4 emissions from wet tropical forest soils. This dataset contains soil chamber fluxes of CO2 and CH4 from 2016 (April 5 through July 18) across a catena in the Luquillo Experimental Forest, Puerto Rico. Soil CO2 fluxes followed the trend of ridge>slope>valley. However, soil CH4 emissions followed the opposite trend, where valley soils served as the major source of CH4 emissions. This dataset can improve our understanding of greenhouse gas (CO2 and CH4) emissions associated with complex topography in wet tropical forest soils.

spatialCoverage.description: Soil chamber data were collected across a catena at the El Verde Research Station of the Luquillo Experimental Forest (LEF) in northeastern Puerto Rico, USA (Figs. 1, 2). Dominant vegetations at the site are composed of mature Tabonuco (Dacryodes excelsa Vahl) and Sierra palm (Prestoea montana) trees (Scatena and Lugo 1995; Wadsworth et al., 1951). The mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation at the site are 23 °C and ~3500 mm, respectively (Scatena, 1989). Soil chamber arrays at ridge, slope, and valley topographic positions are presented in Fig. 2. References Scatena, F. E.: Geomorphology, disturbance, and the soil and vegetation of two subtropical wet steepland watersheds of Puerto Rico, Geomorphology, 13, 199-213, https://doi.org/10.1016/0169-555X(95)00021-V, 1995. measurementTechnique:
We measured soil CO2 and CH4 emissions along the catena using a Cavity Ring-Down Spectroscopy gas analyzer (Picarro G2508, Santa Clara, CA, USA), which was placed in a climate-controlled shed (Figs. 1, 2). We connected our gas analyzer to 12 automated eosAC closed dynamic soil chambers (Pumpanen et al., 2004) using a multiplexer (Eosense Inc., Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, Canada). Soil CO2 and CH4 fluxes were processed using eosAnalyze-AC (v3.5.0) software followed by a series of quality control protocols (O’Connell et al. 2018). See O’Connell et al (2018) for detailed information on the data analysis pipeline. Meteorological data (soil temperature, soil moisture, and oxygen) that accompany this soil chamber data are available from the Luquillo CZO repository (http://criticalzone.org/luquillo/data/dataset/4723/).
